fullDescription:
A reserved seat on the Heritage train over the Hai Van Pass, which is the best stretch of railway in Vietnam.

The line runs along the coast between Da Nang and Hue and climbs the Hai Van, the Ocean Cloud Pass, on a shelf cut into the mountainside. For about forty minutes the track hangs above Lang Co lagoon with the sea directly below the window and the mountain wall on the other side. Jeremy Clarkson called it one of the best coastal roads in the world on Top Gear, and the railway sits above the road with the better view.

The pass is also a real climate line. It blocks the northeast monsoon, so Da Nang on the southern side is often dry and warm while Hue on the northern side is grey and wet on the same afternoon. You watch the weather change through the window.

The Heritage service is the tourist train rather than the ordinary local one: soft seats, air conditioning, large windows built for looking out.

Book the left-hand side travelling from Da Nang to Hue for the sea views, and the right if you are going the other way. This is a one-way ticket, so pick the direction that fits your onward plan rather than doubling back.

Three and a half hours from city centre to city centre, which is faster than the bus and considerably better to look at.

We book with VM Travel Hoi An directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers a one-way E-Heritage train ticket between Da Nang and Hue in either direction, with a reserved soft seat.

Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Forty minutes above Lang Co lagoon on a mountainside shelf
The pass that Top Gear called one of the world's great coastal routes
A real weather line: dry in Da Nang, wet in Hue on the same day
Heritage service: soft seats, air conditioning, big windows
Sit left travelling to Hue, right coming back, for the sea

fullDescription:
Ninety minutes blending your own perfume in Da Nang, and you leave with the bottle.

Perfume is built in three layers and that is what the session teaches. Top notes are the citrus and herbs you smell in the first minutes and then lose. Heart notes are the florals and spices that carry the middle hours. Base notes, the woods, resins and vanillas, are what is still on your skin at the end of the day and what makes one scent linger while another vanishes by lunchtime.

You work through the oils on blotters first, because the nose stops registering a smell after a few minutes and the order you test in changes what you choose. The instructor takes you through the balance, then you mix.

Vietnam grows a good deal of what goes in: cinnamon from Quang Nam, star anise from the north, and agarwood, the resin that makes oud and one of the most expensive raw materials in perfumery.

You take home a 10ml or 30ml bottle of what you made, and because the formula is written down you can have it made again.

Ninety minutes indoors makes this the thing to book when Da Nang's weather turns, which between September and December it regularly does.

We book with Viva Vietnam directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers the guided workshop, all materials and essential oils, and your bottled perfume to take away.

Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Build a scent in three layers: top, heart and base notes
Test on blotters first, because the nose tires within minutes
Vietnamese ingredients: Quang Nam cinnamon, star anise, agarwood
Take home a 10ml or 30ml bottle of your own formula
Indoors, so it holds up when Da Nang's weather turns

fullDescription:
An outdoor show performed on water, half an hour outside Hanoi, with the hillside itself as the set.

The stage is a three-hectare water surface backed by the Thay pagoda mountain, and the performers are around 150 local farmers from the surrounding villages rather than a touring company. They rehearse between seasons and go back to their fields afterwards, which is why the movement in the crowd scenes looks like people rather than choreography.

Six acts run through Vietnamese history and belief: the Buddhist poetry of the north, the scholars and the imperial examinations, the village festivals, the water puppetry that began in these flooded rice fields a thousand years ago.

The technical side is worth knowing about. Sections of stage rise out of the water and sink back, boats appear from behind the trees, and the pagoda behind is lit as part of the set. None of it is on a screen.

Four hours covers the transfer out, the show and the return, so you are back in Hanoi the same evening.

This runs whatever the weather, and evenings in the north are cool from November through February, so take something warm for an outdoor seat.

We book with Up Travel directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers your ticket to the Quintessence of Tonkin show and its six acts.

Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Staged on three hectares of water below Thay pagoda mountain
Around 150 local farmers perform it, not a touring company
Six acts: Buddhist poetry, scholars, festivals, water puppetry
Stage sections rise from the water, nothing on a screen
Outdoor seating, so bring a layer from November to February

fullDescription:
Ninety minutes learning Vietnamese floral arrangement with a working florist, and the arrangement is yours.

Vietnamese arrangement borrows from the Chinese and Japanese traditions and then goes its own way: asymmetry, odd numbers of stems, and a lot of negative space, where a European bouquet fills every gap. The principle is that the space between stems is part of the composition rather than something to hide.

What you work with depends on the season and on the flower market that morning. Saigon runs on lotus, which carries real weight here as the national flower and a Buddhist symbol, plus chrysanthemum, orchid and whatever the market had. The florist explains what each one means before you start, because in Vietnam the meaning changes which flowers belong together and which do not.

You arrange it yourself with guidance rather than watching a demonstration, and Vietnamese tea or juice is served while you work.

The arrangement goes with you at the end.

Indoors and ninety minutes, which makes it easy to fit into an afternoon and reliable when the rain comes down between May and November.

We book with Viva Vietnam directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers all flowers and tools, guidance from a local floral artist, refreshments and your finished arrangement.

Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Asymmetry, odd stem counts and deliberate empty space
Flowers depend on what the market had that morning
Lotus, the national flower, carries real symbolic weight
You arrange it yourself rather than watching a demonstration
Indoors and short, so it survives the wet season afternoons

fullDescription:
Two and a half hours painting your own non la, the Vietnamese conical hat, with an artist who works in English.

The hat itself is the first surprise. It is palm leaf stitched onto a bamboo frame with thread, and the best ones from Hue are made so finely that holding them up to the light shows a poem or a picture worked into the layers, which is where the name non bai tho, the poem hat, comes from. You will be told how yours was made before you put a brush on it.

The painting is acrylic on the leaf surface, which behaves differently from paper: the leaf has a grain and a curve, so strokes pull, and the instructor starts you on a small area to get the feel before you commit to the whole surface.

No drawing experience is expected. Most people work from a traditional motif, lotus, dragon, a Hoi An street, and the artist blocks it out with you.

An apron is provided, and there is drinking water, because two and a half hours bent over a hat in Saigon is warm work.

You take the hat home. It is light and it packs, which is more than can be said for most things bought in Vietnam.

We book with Viva Vietnam directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers an English-speaking artist, one conical hat per person, all painting materials, drinking water and an apron.

Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Palm leaf stitched to a bamboo frame, made the traditional way
Hue's finest hats hide a poem between the layers
Acrylic on leaf pulls differently from paper, so you start small
No drawing experience needed, motifs blocked out with you
Light and packable, unlike most Vietnamese souvenirs

fullDescription:
Two and a half hours cooking in a Hmong home in Ta Van, in the valley below Sapa.

This happens in the village rather than in a Sapa restaurant kitchen, with a Hmong guide, which is the difference. You cook on the household setup and eat what you make at the family table.

Spring rolls are the anchor of the session. Vietnamese rolls are built around whatever is on hand: vermicelli, leafy greens, minced pork, mushroom, wood ear. Rolling them is the part everyone gets wrong at first, because the rice paper softens fast and the whole thing depends on how tightly you roll and how quickly you work.

Ta Van sits in the Muong Hoa valley among the terraced rice fields, a Giay and Hmong village along the river. Getting down there from Sapa town is part of it, and the valley looks entirely different from the ridge.

Hmong cooking in the north leans on things that keep through a cold mountain winter: smoked and dried meat, fermented greens, and the local black cardamom that grows under the forest canopy here and is one of Sapa's actual export crops.

This is the booking for a day when cloud fills the valley, which in Sapa it often does. Nothing about it depends on the view.

We book with Saigonese Trekking House directly, so your place is held before your booking is final. The price covers the workshop with a Hmong guide, all ingredients and the meal you cook.

Minimum one day's notice.
highlights: Cooked in a Hmong home in the village, not a town kitchen
Spring rolls, where the rice paper punishes slow hands
Ta Van in the Muong Hoa valley, among the rice terraces
Northern mountain cooking: smoked meat, fermented greens
Black cardamom, grown under the forest canopy around Sapa
